summary: Defines the NSIS Signaling Layer Protocol for NATs and firewalls, letting hosts signal along the data path to configure them for application flows. For example, it can get a host behind a NAT a public address. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A firewall or a NAT on the path between two computers can stop their conversation, because neither device was told that this particular traffic should be allowed. RFC 5973 lets the application itself say so. The request travels along the same path the data will take, and each firewall and NAT along the way reads it, opens the right hole, and passes it on. When the conversation ends, the holes close again on their own.

questions: how do nat and firewall nslp work
external message for receivers behind nat
subtitle: Signal to middleboxes along the data path to open firewall pinholes and create NAT bindings.

tldr.problem: Applications behind NATs and firewalls cannot always reach each other, because those devices block or rewrite traffic they do not recognise.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol sends CREATE and EXTERNAL messages along the data path. Each middlebox intercepts them, installs firewall rules and NAT bindings on the fly, and forwards the message on.
tldr.outcome: Applications can ask the devices along their path for the permission they need, instead of the administrator pre-configuring every rule. The protocol is Experimental.

today: RFC 5973 is an Experimental document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It sits inside the NSIS framework: the transport layer is RFC 5971, the framework itself is RFC 4080, and the companion protocol for quality-of-service signalling is RFC 5974. The memo also notes that the deployment and extensibility issues described in those documents apply to it.

sections.title: Why Signal Along the Data Path
sections.content:
Firewalls and NATs have been on the Internet for many years and will remain there. Firewalls protect networks against certain kinds of attack; NATs give a network a virtual extension of the IP address space. Both can stand in the way of an application, because they only let through traffic from a limited set of applications, typically those with static and predictable properties such as ordinary web traffic. Applications with more dynamic behaviour, such as IP telephony and most peer-to-peer applications, create traffic that cannot traverse them without help.

Several fixes have been proposed and are in use. Application-level gateways inside the firewall or NAT configure the device dynamically. Middlebox communication puts the gateway outside the device and drives it with a separate protocol, described in RFC 3303. Session Traversal Utilities for NAT, RFC 5389, is another workaround. The memo says all of these bring their own problems, such as a dependence on the kind of NAT in use or on a particular network topology.

The approach here is to signal along the data path, so that the signalling messages follow exactly the same route the data packets take. That property is already familiar from quality-of-service signalling, and the Resource Reservation Protocol in RFC 2205 is an example of a path-coupled protocol in use. A source host sends a signalling message towards its data destination; every NATFW-enabled device along the path intercepts it, processes it and configures itself, and afterwards the data flow can pass through all of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Existing fixes each need the application to be understood by the firewall or the NAT, which means one piece of work per protocol. This memo takes the other approach: the application asks the devices on its path to make an exception, and the request travels on the same route the data will take.

sections.title: The Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
Middleboxes are typically found at enterprise network borders, inside enterprise networks, and at mobile network gateways, and they are usually placed nearer the edge of a network than in its core. Firewalls and NATs may appear at these locations alone or combined. The memo walks through the resulting scenarios, each assuming that every middlebox implements the protocol.

A firewall-traversal scenario has a firewall at each end with the public Internet between them, and each firewall must provide a traversal service so that the signalling message can reach the other end. A scenario with NATs at both ends has the outermost NAT on each side, known as the edge-NAT, connected to the public Internet. Other scenarios place the private network on the sender's side, on the receiver's side, or have both end hosts behind twice-NATs, where two translators sit in series. There are also scenarios for both end hosts behind the same NAT and for a multihomed network, with or without a firewall.

The memo notes two basic situations. When both the sender and the receiver are protocol-aware, end-to-end signalling is possible. When only one side is aware, the protocol uses a proxy mode in which the NSIS-aware middleboxes on the path provide the service on behalf of the other end. The sections are described as examples rather than a limit on the scope of the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists the places the devices can sit: a firewall at each end, a NAT at each end, a NAT at one end only, two NATs in series, both computers behind one NAT, and networks with several links. For each one it shows how the signalling reaches the devices it has to reach.

sections.title: Policy Rules and the Basic Protocol
sections.content:
Policy rules bound to a signalling session are the building blocks the middleboxes work with. A firewall's rule is usually a 5-tuple and an action such as allow or deny, where the tuple carries the source and destination addresses, the transport protocol and the source and destination port numbers. A NAT's rule is the action of translating an address, plus the mapping information, in the simplest case an internal and an external address. The protocol specifies two actions: deny, which drops every matching packet, and allow, which forwards every matching packet.

The rule carried in the signalling is an abstraction of the rule the device will really install. For a pure firewall one or more filter rules must be created; for a pure NAT one or more bindings; and in a box that does both, the rule must be mapped onto filter rules and bindings in the right order, which decides whether the firewall rules carry public or private addresses. The exact mapping depends on the implementation.

Messages travel over GIST, the implementation of the NSIS transport layer described in RFC 5971. The initiator is the node that starts the exchange, the responder is the node that receives it, and forwarders are the nodes in between. At least the initiator and the responder must implement the protocol; a forwarder only needs to when it provides a middlebox function, and one with no relevant function simply passes the messages along.
sections.plainLanguage: Each device matches packets against a rule that says which traffic to let through and which to drop. The rule that travels in the signalling describes what is wanted in general terms, and each device turns it into whatever form its own engine uses.

sections.title: Signaling Sessions and Their Lifetime
sections.content:
The protocol runs on soft state. Whatever is installed or reserved on a middlebox expires after a while and is then uninstalled, and the resources bound to it are freed. To stop state that is still needed from being removed early, the initiator has to ask for the session to be extended, and the protocol also provides an explicit way to delete a session.

A session is identified by a session ID that the initiator generates before sending the first message. The ID must be a cryptographically random number, so that it is not guessable by third parties, and it is not carried in any of the protocol's own messages but passed to the transport layer. A session has four conceptual states at each node. Pending means the session has been created and the node is waiting for a response, and it becomes dead if no response arrives within the locally granted lifetime. Established means the signalling succeeded and the lifetime is counted from that moment, and the session becomes dead if no refresh arrives within the granted lifetime. Dead means the session has timed out or an error response has been received, and it can be deleted. Transitory means an asynchronous message has arrived; the session should not be deleted for at least 30 seconds, so that the initiator can reuse the part of it that a route change did not affect.

The lifetime is chosen by the initiator before any message is sent, and the memo recommends taking into account the number of lost refresh messages the forwarders should cope with, the end-to-end delay, the risk of a session being hijacked, how long the application needs the flow, the load on the signalling plane, and how long an unused session may safely linger. Forwarders and the responder must not trigger refreshes themselves; that is the initiator's job.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing is opened forever. Each session has a lifetime, and the initiator has to keep saying it is still needed. The session moves through a small number of states, and a session that has failed is cleaned up after a short hold so that the initiator can reuse what still works.

sections.title: The Four Message Types
sections.content:
Every message begins with a common 32-bit header holding the message type, a proxy flag, an end-to-end flag and two reserved fields, and the reserved fields must be set to zero and ignored on receipt. The four message types are CREATE, EXTERNAL, RESPONSE and NOTIFY. A message with any other type is answered with an error response of class 'Protocol error' and code 'Illegal message type'.

CREATE is a request for creating, changing, refreshing and deleting sessions, and it opens the data path from the sender to the receiver. It carries the signaling session lifetime, the extended flow information and the message sequence number objects as mandatory, plus optionally the nonce and the ICMP types objects. EXTERNAL is a request for reserving, changing, refreshing and deleting external sessions. It is used to reserve an external address and port at a NAT, to tell firewalls about a protocol-aware receiver, and to block incoming traffic at an inbound firewall. It carries the session lifetime, the message sequence number, the extended flow information and the data terminal information objects, with the nonce, ICMP types and external binding address objects optional.

NOTIFY is the asynchronous message, used by one node to alert another about an event such as a failure. RESPONSE is the answer to a CREATE or EXTERNAL request, and it must not be generated for any other message. Every RESPONSE carries an information code object with an error class and a response code. The classes are 'Success' for a successful response, 'Informational' for a message that carries information rather than an answer, and everything else is an error response.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of message. CREATE asks for the path to be opened. EXTERNAL asks for a public address to be set aside, or for unwanted traffic to be blocked. RESPONSE is the answer. NOTIFY reports something that happened later, such as a failure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says security is of major concern, particularly for firewall traversal, and it points at the threats to NSIS described in RFC 4081. It does not treat the protocol as a two-party exchange, because several nodes take part. Three relationships are described: a peer-to-peer one between neighbouring nodes, an intra-domain one where middleboxes share a policy decision point or trust each other, and an end-to-middle one where the far end needs to authorise the initiator as well.

Between neighbouring nodes the memo recommends data origin authentication, replay protection, integrity protection and, optionally, confidentiality, using the authentication and key exchange mechanisms that GIST provides. Almost all the threats can be prevented by a mutually authenticated transport-layer connection and by the neighbouring nodes authorising each other. The protocol relies on an established security association between neighbouring peers to stop unauthorised nodes from changing or deleting installed state.

Between non-neighbouring nodes the session identifier is used to show ownership of a session. Because it is random, an off-path attacker would have to learn it, although a former on-path node that has become off-path can still attack. Some scenarios may also use authorisation tokens, which associate the decision made by another protocol, such as SIP or network access authentication, with this signalling. The memo closes with a note on UNilateral Self-Address Fixing: because the endpoints take part in allocating, maintaining and deleting addresses and ports at the middlebox, the protocol is offered as a long-term alternative to the workarounds discussed in RFC 3424.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a hole in a firewall is something an attacker would like to cause, so the signalling is protected between neighbouring devices and the identifier that ties a session to its owner is made unpredictable. Where a decision has already been made elsewhere, a token can carry that decision along with the request.
